control: Burgh and castle under David I; mint by 1153.
Castle handed to Henry II under the Treaty of Falaise (Dec. 1174); returned by Richard I in the Quitclaim of Canterbury (Dec. 1189).
Burnt by King John in January 1216. Site of the Great Cause hearings, 1291-92, under Edward I.
Taken by Edward I, 30 March 1296. In 1297 the Scots held the town for a time but not the castle (to verify).
Taken by Robert I in April 1318 (CDS iii, nos 693-94; CPL ii, 420, 429). English siege of 1319 failed (CDS iii, no. 668).

Surrendered to Edward III on 20 July 1333, the day after Halidon Hill (Foedera syllabus i). Interruptions: Scots held the town (not the castle) Nov. 1355-Jan. 1356; castle seized Nov. 1378 and again 1384; held by the Percy rebels until July 1405.
Surrendered by Margaret of Anjou to the Scots, 25 April 1461.
Castle surrendered to Richard, duke of Gloucester, 24 August 1482. English thereafter.
interruptions: Scots under Wallace take the town (castle holds)
Castle seized by a small Scottish party, retaken by Northumberland
Castle taken by the Scots; bought back by Northumberland
Held for the rebel earl of Northumberland until Henry IV arrives

sieges.x: John takes the castle, burns castle and town, and breaks the bridge behind his army.

sieges.held: Scotland (men of Fife sent to defend it)
sieges.x: Scots burn two English ships in the harbour; the English cross the ditch and take the town on Good Friday. Thirty Flemings hold the Red Hall until evening and are burnt in it. The castle yields the same night. Reported deaths range from 4,000 (Langtoft) upwards.
sieges.r: Guisborough (Hamilton) ii, c. p. 98; Langtoft (Wright) ii, pp. 234-35; Fordun (Skene), pp. 317-18; Hardyng (Ellis), p. 288

sieges.by: Henry de Haliburton for William Wallace
sieges.x: After Stirling Bridge the English leave the town waste; Wallace's men occupy it but not the castle, and leave it empty when the English return.
Night attack with rope ladders and iron hooks; a barking dog gives the alarm.

sieges.by: James Douglas and the earl of March for Robert I
sieges.held: England (the mayor and community, by contract)
sieges.x: Peter (Sim) of Spalding lets the Scots onto the wall; the castle holds out eleven weeks and then capitulates for want of relief.
sieges.r: Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 57; Fordun (Skene), p. 339; Barbour (Mackenzie), Bk XVII; CDS iii, nos 693-94

sieges.x: Engines, the "Sow" and an assault from the sea; Crab's crane breaks the Sow. The siege is raised after the Scots defeat a Yorkshire levy at Myton.
sieges.r: Barbour (Mackenzie), Bk XVII; Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 64; CDS iii, no. 668; Fordun (Skene), pp. 339-41

sieges.held: Scotland (Alexander Seton, William Keith; the earl of March in the castle)
sieges.x: Siege by land and sea from the second week of Lent; guns used against the town (the Brut); a truce with hostages; Thomas Seton hanged; the relieving army is destroyed at Halidon Hill on 19 July and the town surrenders on terms.
sieges.r: Scalacronica (Maxwell), pp. 93-95; Fordun (Skene), p. 347; Lanercost (Maxwell), pp. 270-81; Brut (Brie), 1333 chapters; Scott 1888, p. 53

sieges.by: Thomas Stewart, earl of Angus, and the earl of March
sieges.x: The Scots take the town by night; the castle holds. Edward III comes north and the town is surrendered to him on 24 Jan. 1356.
The castle is taken by night during a truce; it is soon retaken and the Scots in it are killed.
Money paid to the under-keeper opens the castle while the earl is at Parliament; he recovers it.
The first shot from a great gun breaks a tower and the garrison surrenders.
The Scots try again for Berwick during Henry VI's minority.
Messengers are paid for news "at the raising of the siege of Berwick".

sieges.by: Richard of Gloucester and the earl of Northumberland
sieges.held: Scotland (Patrick Hepburn of Hailes in the castle)
sieges.x: The town is retaken; the castle surrenders later in the month.

sieges_region.x: Repeated Scottish sieges of the bishop of Durham's castle, held by Thomas Gray the elder; relieved by Percy and Neville.
Scots besiege Queen Philippa in Bamburgh to draw Edward III from Berwick; the siege is abandoned after Halidon.
sieges_region.r: Minot (Hall), notes to poem I; Walsingham (Riley) appendix

sieges_region.x: Edward I takes Stirling after a long siege, the last before Wallace's capture.
At Berwick, early in May 1296, Edward I hears that the Scots have taken Dunbar castle; the English win the battle there.

freiris.title: The Freiris of Berwik
freiris.ref: Bannatyne MS (Edinburgh, NLS Adv. MS 1.1.6), fol. 348; ed. Hunterian Club, Bannatyne iv (1896), pp. 1004-05; also in the Maitland Folio. Anonymous; sometimes ascribed to Dunbar.
lines: At Tweidis mowth thair standis a nobill toun
For it is wallit weill abowt with stane, / And dowbill stankis castin mony ane
And syne the castell is so strang and wicht, / With strait towris and turattis he on hicht
The port cules most subtelly to fall
The grit croce kirk, and eik the Masone Dew
The Jacobene freiris of the quhyt hew, / The Carmeleitis, and the monkis eik
The four ordouris wer nocht for to seik, / Thay wer all in this toun dwelling
freiris.note: "Grit croce kirk" may be the parish church of Holy Trinity or the church of the Trinitarians; the identification is left open. "Jacobene" (Dominican) friars are usually black, not white; the poem's colour is its own.

town.name: Berwick Castle
town.note: Royal castle on the high ground west of the town, its site now cut by the railway station (1840s). Great hall where judgement in the Great Cause was given, 17 Nov. 1292 (verify). Constables and keepers listed under Governance.
town.refs: CPR 1292-1301, p. 437 (John de Burdon, constable and sheriff, 1299); CDS iii, no. 121 (John Spark, constable, 1309); CDS iv, no. 246 (Robert de Boynton, constable, 1377)

town.name: White Wall and Water Tower
town.note: Wall running from the castle down the slope to a tower at the river, closing the castle to the Tweed. The "Constable Tower" ruin on the modern map lies on this line.
town.refs: OSM (Constable Tower); Speed 1610 shows the wall and a tower at the waterside (his letter B).

town.name: Bell Tower
town.note: Watch tower on the line of the medieval north wall, rebuilt in 1577. Marks how far north the medieval circuit ran compared with the Elizabethan walls.

town.name: Holy Trinity parish church
town.note: The parish church of medieval Berwick; the present building (1650-52) stands on or near the medieval site. Berwick lay in the Scottish diocese of St Andrews throughout the English occupation.
town.refs: CPL i-iv (diocese of St Andrews); Speed 1610 (his letter L, church with crosses)

town.name: Bridge over the Tweed
town.note: A stone bridge was lost to floods in the 1290s; later bridges were timber until the present Old Bridge (1611-24). The Trinitarian friars were called "of the Bridge of Berwick". The ferry and passage tolls between Berwick and Tweedmouth were disputed with the bishop of Durham, 1366-75.
town.refs: CPL iv, 253 (Trinitarians of the Bridge); CDS iv, nos 129, 157; CPR 1364-67, p. 384 (keeping of the passage, 1367); CDS iii, no. 1443 (ferry until a horse and foot bridge was built)

town.name: Marygate ("Saynt Marigat")
town.note: Main street of the town. Named in a 1335 inquisition of rents ("Saynt Marigat").

town.name: Briggate (Bridge Street)
town.note: Waterfront street by the bridge. Coldingham Priory bought "bordes de Estland" (Baltic timber) delivered to the Bryggat of Berwick.

town.name: Seagate ("Segate")
town.note: Street named in 1334: John Crab, burgess of Berwick, granted his tenement called "le Withalle" in Segate street, formerly James of Cologne's. Exact line of the medieval street not established; placed near Sandgate.

town.name: Red Hall of the Flemings (Aula Rubra)
town.note: Hall of the Flemish merchants, defended and burnt with its occupants when Edward I took the town, 30 March 1296. Site unknown; the marker is a placeholder near the waterfront.
town.refs: Chronicle accounts (Lanercost, Guisborough, Bower) to verify

town.name: Watergate
town.note: Gate to the quay. Its keeping was granted for life to William de Risceby, 1359, at 12d. a day paid by the chamberlain; later a payment by the chamberlain for its custody (1378). Position approximate.

town.name: Quay and harbour
town.note: Port of the wool trade. Berwick shipped about one third of Scotland's wool exports, 1327-33, about forty customed sailings a year.

town.name: Maison Dieu hospital
town.note: Hospital ("House of God") with a chapel; indulgence for visitors on the Assumption and feasts of SS. Andrew and John. A "Mesondew croft" is named in 1335. Position approximate (Hide Hill).

town.name: Tweedmouth
town.note: South bank of the Tweed, in the bishop of Durham's liberty of Norhamshire, so in England when Berwick was Scottish.
town.refs: CDS iv, no. 129 (rights of the bishop in the Tweed between Norham and Tweedmouth)

town.name: Halidon Hill
town.note: Battle of 19 July 1333, two miles north-west of the town. Edward III vowed before it to found a house of thirteen Black Benedictines if he won.
town.refs: CDS iii, no. 1277; Foedera syllabus i (surrender of Berwick, 20 July)

unplaced.name: Franciscans (Friars Minor)
unplaced.note: Received 20 marks yearly of alms through the chamberlain of Berwick (Foedera syllabus i, Robert de Inghale chamberlain). Complaint against Kelso abbey with the Friars Minor of Roxburgh (CPL ii, 503).

unplaced.name: Dominicans (Friars Preachers)
unplaced.note: Their first site was too far from the town for confession, sermons and visiting the sick; in 1289 the pope allowed them to buy the place left by the Friars of Penitence (Friars of the Sack).

unplaced.name: Friars of the Sack (Friars of Penitence)
unplaced.note: Had left their house in the town by 1289.

unplaced.name: Carmelites
unplaced.note: Isabella, countess of Buchan, was moved from her cage to the Carmelite house at Berwick (to verify).

unplaced.name: Trinitarians "of the Bridge of Berwick"
unplaced.note: Named in a letter of Clement VII (Avignon, 1386) as adherents of "Bartholomew, sometime archbishop of Bari" (Urban VI), the Roman pope of the Schism, and so to be removed from the Scottish church of Ketins.

unplaced.name: Schools of Berwick
unplaced.note: A "master of the schools of Berwick, in the diocese of St Andrews" was named as papal judge-delegate in a Galloway dower suit, 1243.

unplaced.name: Cistercian nuns (South Berwick)
unplaced.note: The nuns were in the town when it was surrendered in 1333; their rent was to be restored "as held since K. Alexander's time".

speed_notes.name: Medieval wall circuit (north-west)
speed_notes.note: Speed shows the long medieval circuit, running from the castle to the sea, still standing outside the smaller Elizabethan walls of 1558-70.

speed_notes.name: Elizabethan walls
speed_notes.note: Bastioned trace begun in 1558, later than the period of the chapter; it cut the medieval town down to its southern half.

speed_notes.name: Shore tower
speed_notes.note: Tower where the medieval wall met the shore on the sea side.

speed_notes.name: Gate in the north wall
speed_notes.note: Arched gate by the church (Speed's letter Z).

region.name: Berwick-upon-Tweed
region.note: Royal burgh, chief of the Four Burghs before 1296.

region.name: Norham Castle
region.note: Castle of the bishops of Durham on the Tweed. Edward I received the Scottish magnates here in 1291. Thomas Gray the elder and the younger were constables (younger from 1345).

region.name: Heton (Castle Heaton)
region.note: Caput of the Gray family in Norhamshire, held of the bishops of Durham; forfeited by Robert Gray, who died in the Scottish allegiance, and acquired by Thomas Gray the elder by 1312.

region.name: Upsettlington
region.note: Scottish bank opposite Norham, where the Scottish claimants met Edward I in 1291 (to verify).

region.name: Wark on Tweed
region.note: English border castle; its garrison is named with Berwick's in 1300 (CPR 1292-1301, p. 491).

region.name: Etal
region.note: Castle of Robert Manners, constable of Norham 1327-45, a couple of miles down the Till from Heton.

region.name: Birgham
region.note: Treaty of Birgham, July 1290, for the marriage of Margaret of Norway and Edward of Caernarfon (to verify).

region.name: Coldstream
region.note: Cistercian nunnery on the Tweed.

region.name: Roxburgh
region.note: Royal burgh and castle, one of the Four Burghs with Berwick, Edinburgh and Stirling; English-held for long periods with Berwick.
region.refs: CDS iv, no. 252 (Thomas Percy, warden of Roxburgh, 1377)

region.name: Kelso Abbey
region.note: Tironensian abbey with property in Berwick; dispute with the Friars Minor of Berwick and Roxburgh.

region.name: Melrose Abbey
region.note: Cistercian abbey; major wool producer for the Flemish market.

region.name: Dryburgh Abbey
region.note: Premonstratensian abbey.

region.name: Jedburgh
region.note: Abbey and castle; English garrison with Berwick and Roxburgh in the 1380s-1400s.

region.name: Coldingham Priory
region.note: Cell of Durham Cathedral Priory; bought Baltic timber shipped to Berwick and kept its own coaster. The prior was the Scottish commissioner for truce complaints in 1432, the mayor of Berwick the English one.

region.name: Ayton
region.note: A March day was appointed at Ayton for 12 June 1381.

region.name: Lamberton
region.note: Manor near Berwick granted with the barony of Lindsay in the town to William de Coucy, 1335.

region.name: Earlston (Erceldoune)
region.note: Home of Thomas of Erceldoune ("the Rhymer"), whose prophecies circulated in English manuscripts.

region.name: Duns
region.note: Berwickshire; John Duns Scotus is named from it (to verify).

region.name: Dunbar
region.note: Castle of the earls of March. Battle of Dunbar, 27 April 1296, four weeks after the sack of Berwick (to verify).

region.name: Haddington
region.note: Wallace and Andrew Moray wrote from here to Lübeck and Hamburg, 11 Oct. 1297 (to verify).

region.name: Edinburgh
region.note: Thomas Gray began the Scalacronica as a prisoner in Edinburgh Castle, 1355-56.

region.name: Bamburgh
region.note: Royal castle; a Berwick ship, la Margarete, was sunk between Bamburgh and Berwick in 1359.

region.name: Holy Island (Lindisfarne)
region.note: Edward I wrote to London from Holy Island in March 1296, days before the assault on Berwick.
region.refs: Calendar of Letter-Book B (introduction), p. iii

region.name: Alnwick
region.note: Percy castle from 1309; the Percy earls were wardens and captains of Berwick for most of 1377-1461.

region.name: Warkworth
region.note: Percy castle; Henry IV dated letters here in July 1405 on the way to Berwick.

region.name: Homildon (Humbleton) Hill
region.note: Battle of 14 Sept. 1402, won by the Percys (to verify).

region.name: Otterburn
region.note: Battle of Aug. 1388; Henry Percy (Hotspur), late warden of Berwick, captured (to verify).

region.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
region.note: Port and staging point for the English in the March; Berwick merchants also shipped from the Tyne.

region.name: Durham
region.note: Cathedral priory (owner of Coldingham) and the bishops of Durham, lords of Norhamshire and Islandshire.

region.name: Neville's Cross
region.note: 17 Oct. 1346; David II captured by John de Coupland, later warden of Berwick.
region.refs: King 2000, p. 226; Foedera syllabus i (Coupland warden)

region.name: Stirling
region.note: One of the Four Burghs; English garrison supplied by sea through Berwick in the 1300s-1340s.

region.name: Carlisle
region.note: Counterpart of Berwick on the West March.

region.name: North Berwick (a different place)
region.note: Cistercian nunnery in East Lothian whose charters are in the Berwick folder. Not Berwick-upon-Tweed.

events.x: William the Lion, captured at Alnwick, hands Berwick castle and others to Henry II.
events.r: CDS i, no. 139 and introduction (only Roxburgh, Edinburgh and Berwick were actually delivered); Fordun (Skene), p. 261

events.x: Richard I releases the Scottish castles for 10,000 marks.
events.r: Fordun (Skene), p. 267 (text of Richard I's letter); CDS i, no. 196; Langtoft (Wright) ii, p. 32

events.t: A castle at Tweedmouth "to destroy Berwick"
events.x: King John begins a castle at Tweedmouth; William the Lion twice pulls it down, and the treaty of 1209 orders it razed and never rebuilt.
Raid in reprisal for Alexander II's support of the rebel barons.
events.r: Fordun (Skene), p. 279: John "burnt down Berwick Castle, together with the town" and broke the bridge

events.x: A "master of the schools of Berwick" is named as a papal judge-delegate in a Galloway dower suit.
Alexander II tells Robert Bernham, mayor of Berwick, not to impede foreign merchants coming to buy the wool of Coldingham Priory.

events.t: Statutes of the Guild of Berwick
events.x: Ordinances of the merchant guild, made under the mayor Robert of Bernham; added to until 1294.
events.r: Scott 1888 (Guild history), printing the statutes in Appendix VII; Robert Bernham mayor in 1238 and 1249

events.x: Lanercost calls him "as much a knight as a burgess". Ancestor of the chronicler Thomas Gray.
Scottish bishops and earls meet at Berwick, English commissioners at Tweedmouth, to settle border disputes.

events.t: Dower of Margaret of Flanders on Berwick
events.x: Margaret, daughter of Guy count of Flanders and widow of Prince Alexander, assigned 1,300 marks a year from the revenues of Berwick.
Pope allows the Friars Preachers to buy the place left by the Friars of Penitence, their own being too far from the town.
Edward I binds himself to pay 3,000 marks at Berwick to the keepers of Scotland unless Margaret of Norway arrives by All Saints.
Relaxation of penance for visitors to the chapel of the House of God at Berwick on the Assumption and the feasts of SS. Andrew and the two Johns.

events.t: Edward I at Berwick: the Great Cause
events.x: Letters patent dated at Berwick in June and August 1291. The men of Florence, count of Holland, a claimant, are robbed in Lincolnshire on their way to the king in Scotland.
Given in the great hall of Berwick castle.
events.r: Fordun (Skene), p. 313 (sentence given at Berwick); Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 9

events.x: The bridge across the Tweed falls in a flood, "because the arches were too low", nine years after it was built.
His dead father appears as a Franciscan, warning that the people of Berwick have neglected the alms he began for St Francis. Told in the Lanercost chronicle.
The defenders mock Edward I from the walls: "Wenes Kyng Edward, wiþ his longe shankes, forto wyn Berwik... gas pikes him! and when he haþ hit, gas diche him!" The English verses answer in kind.
events.r: Brut (Brie), ch. 168; Langtoft (Wright) ii, pp. 234-35 ("Pyket him, / an dyket him")

events.x: The town is taken on Good Friday; the Flemings defend their Red Hall and are burnt in it.
events.r: Guisborough (Hamilton) ii, c. p. 98 (thirty Flemings in the Aula Rubea burnt in it); Langtoft (Wright) ii, pp. 234-35; Fordun (Skene), pp. 317-18; Brut (Brie), ch. 168

events.x: Edward I writes to the citizens of London from Berwick; parliament summoned by writ dated at Berwick, 26 Aug. 1296.
Edward I has a deep ditch dug between the Scots and the town, "large and wide", in mockery of the Scots' song.
events.r: Walsingham (Riley) i, p. 56; Langtoft (Wright) ii, p. 234

events.x: Scottish landholders swear fealty to Edward I at Berwick.
events.r: Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 16; Walsingham (Riley) i, p. 60 (parliament at Berwick, fealties and homages)

events.t: Foreign merchants and the new regime
events.x: Safe-conduct dated at Berwick for John le Parchemener of Louvain, merchant of Brabant, on condition he takes no goods to France; complaint of merchants of Lübeck and Dortmund heard.
The English set up an exchequer for Scotland at Berwick, with Hugh de Cressingham as treasurer and Walter of Amundesham as chancellor.

events.t: Survey of the town and port
events.x: Commission with Hugh de Cressingham, treasurer of Scotland, on the site and state of the town and port of Berwick.
Citizens of London with burgesses of twenty-two towns summoned to advise the king on a new constitution for the town.
events.r: Cal. Letter-Book C, p. 25 n. 1 (citing Stubbs, Select Charters)

events.x: Wallace and Andrew Moray tell the merchants of Lübeck and Hamburg that the kingdom has been recovered and their trade is welcome.
events.r: Not found in the editions searched

events.x: After Stirling Bridge, Warenne abandons Berwick "leaving the town waste"; Wallace sends Henry de Haliburton to seize it; he leaves it empty when the English return.
Philip de Vernay keeper of the town and coroner; John de Burdon constable of the castle and sheriff of the county of Berwick.
Edward I assembles an army at Berwick at Midsummer; London ordered to send food and harness there.
events.r: CPR 1292-1301, p. 578; Cal. Letter-Book C, pp. 91, 96

events.x: Edward I has the town "surrounded with a stone wall".
After his execution in London a quarter of Wallace's body is displayed at Berwick.
events.r: Scott 1888, ch. II (his left arm exposed at Berwick)

events.t: The countess of Buchan in a cage
events.x: Isabella MacDuff, who crowned Robert I, is held in a cage at Berwick castle for about four years.
events.r: Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 29 ("a little wooden chamber in a tower of the castle of Berwick with sparred sides"); CDS ii, no. 1851 (order of 7 Nov. 1306)

events.x: The king's brother and others, taken at Kildrummy, are tried and executed at Berwick.
events.r: Scalacronica (Maxwell), p. 29; Fordun (Skene), p. 335; CDS ii, introduction

events.x: The king and queen stay from November 1310 to July 1311; 66 letters patent dated at Berwick in 1311, and London receives writs dated there.
events.r: CDS iii, no. 177; CPR 1307-13; Cal. Letter-Book D, pp. 240-69

events.x: Stralsund arrests goods of Roger Bishop, burgess of Berwick, for a Stralsund ship burnt at Berwick by the admiral John de Botetourt.

events.t: Rope ladders and a barking dog
events.x: Robert I tries to take the castle by night with rope ladders hooked to the wall; a dog's barking raises the alarm. The Lanercost writer saw the ladders "with my own eyes".
Writ dated at Berwick, four days after Bannockburn, telling London to ignore commands under the king's privy seal, which has been lost.
Burgesses of Roxburgh who fled to Berwick, Bamburgh and Newcastle complain that the bailiffs there will not let them bake or trade, but treat them as strangers.
London sends 120 crossbowmen, named in the Letter-Book, with their arms carted north in seventeen to eighteen days.

events.t: A Berwick ship arrested in Norway
events.x: Edward II asks Haakon of Norway for redress: a Berwick vessel carrying Flemish goods worth £527 was driven into "Wyke" and arrested. Haakon replies from Bergen, 18 July 1316.
Maurice de Berkeley, warden, reports the misery of the garrison and community from scarcity.
Burgesses licensed under the town seal to buy corn in France and wine in Gascony; La Trinite of Berwick sails to Gascony.
Antonio Pessagno of Genoa contracts to supply 17,000 qrs of flour and 2,600 tuns of wine, delivered at Berwick, Newcastle and Skinburness, and five galleys.

events.t: The burgesses keep their own town
events.x: The town is delivered to the mayor, bailiffs and community, who undertake its defence for a year for 6,000 marks; hostages for the burgesses received at York.
Edward II blames the mayor and community, "by whose carelessness" the Scots entered. The pope excommunicates Robert for breaking the truce.
"Liege people who were burgesses of Berwick" ask to live and trade freely in England and to have their children released from prison.

events.t: Robert de Neville killed near Berwick
events.x: Gray blames "the false traitors of the March" for his death "par couyne".

Pay sheet of the besieging army: contingents from York, Barnard Castle, Nottingham, 2,400 foot from North and South Wales, and 120 archers and 20 crossbowmen of the "late English garrison". The siege is lifted.
events.r: CDS iii, no. 668; Cal. Letter-Book E, p. 30

events.x: The besiegers bring up a covered engine, the "Sow"; the defenders' crane, built on John Crab's advice, smashes it; a seaborne assault on the walls fails.
The Bruce credits the Flemish engineer John Crab with the town's defence in 1319.
events.r: Barbour (Mackenzie), Bk XVII, ll. 239-44 ("Johne Crab, a Flemyne... of gret subtilite") and ll. 600-710 (the crane and the Sow)

events.x: David, son of Robert I, marries Joan, Edward III's sister, at Berwick. Christopher of Cologne, burgess of Berwick, complains that his Picard wheat, shipped at St-Valery for the household, was lost; the warden of the Cinque Ports is ordered to make amends.
Stephen de Forburg, burgess of Berwick, pays 4,000 florins of the tenth collected in Scotland to the papal camera through the Azzaiuoli of Florence.
Hostage son of the keeper Alexander Seton hanged before the walls during the siege.
events.r: Fordun (Skene), p. 347 (Thomas, son of the warden Alexander Seton, given as hostage); Scott 1888, p. 53 (hanged for breach of the agreement)

events.x: Edward III defeats the relieving army; the town is surrendered next day by Patrick, earl of March, and William Keith, warden. 27 letters patent dated at Berwick that July.
events.r: Foedera syllabus i; CPR 1330-34; CDS iii, no. 1277

events.t: Scottish clergy expelled; the friars' books
events.x: Edward III orders all clergy of Scottish birth out of Berwick. The departing Scottish friars entertain their English replacements at dinner while others pack the convent's books, chalices and vestments in silk and carry them off.

Henry Percy made warden with Thomas Gray (the chronicler's father) under him; William de Burnton, formerly mayor of Newcastle, made mayor; justices to find which Englishmen had been disinherited in the town and restore their houses.
John Crab, burgess, grants his tenement "le Withalle" in Seagate street, formerly James of Cologne's, and a garden.
Burgesses who surrendered with the town ask to be released from prison at Newcastle. Answer: Scots living at Newcastle may trade within the realm.
57 letters patent dated at Berwick in October 1335 alone, during the campaigns for Edward Balliol.
Forty customed sailings; eight ships carry 720 sacks for a syndicate led by the mayor, John of Chilton. Only two foreign merchants trade at Berwick.
Chilton's Zeeland-bound cargo on La Eleyne of Ravenser is released on the claim that it was bound for Ireland.
William de Kelleseye appointed chancellor of Berwick and the king's other lands in Scotland at £50 a year and the fees of the seal.
John de Mowbray, warden for a year: 120 men-at-arms, 100 hobelars, 200 archers, 48 watchmen and a master engineer.
During a truce twelve chosen Scottish knights come to joust at Berwick; two are killed, and one of the earl of Derby's knights.
Resident burgesses may buy 200 sacks of wool in the English March and ship them to Flanders at half a mark custom a sack, quit of the 40s. subsidy.
The poor commons of Berwick petition that the burgesses are so few and impoverished that the town cannot be kept.
Berwick merchants' ships from Sluys (la Marie, la Nicholas of Nieuport) are driven ashore in Suffolk; Christopher of Cologne among the merchants.
The mayor and people complain that wool from the king's lordship in Scotland, once shipped from Berwick, now goes to the Scots because of the embargo.
Thomas Gray, constable of Norham, captured in 1355 and held in Edinburgh Castle, starts his chronicle there.
The town, not the castle, is taken; Edward III recovers it in January 1356. French knights took part (to verify).
events.r: Fordun (Skene), pp. 361-63 (earl of Angus takes the town; castle holds; surrendered to Edward III in Feb.); Knighton (Lumby) ii (surrender, 24 Jan. 1356)

events.x: Terms for the release of David II for 100,000 marks; instalments of the ransom were later received at Berwick by its warden.
events.r: Foedera syllabus i (Coupland, warden of Berwick, to receive instalments)

events.x: Keeping of the Watergate granted for life to William de Risceby, 12d. a day from the chamberlain.
The bishop of Durham complains that the chamberlain John de Bolton has taken the ferry and the passage of ships on both banks as belonging to the town.
Inquisition of Queenborough: a mariner sailing London to Berwick is paid 8s., against 4s. to Newcastle and 13s. 4d. to Scania.
events.r: Black Book of the Admiralty i, pp. 140-41

events.x: A small Scottish party under Alexander Ramsay takes the castle; the earl of Northumberland retakes it.
events.r: Fordun (Skene), p. 371: taken "by night, during a truce, by some of the meaner sort", soon retaken and the Scots in it slain. The leader's name (Alexander Ramsay) is from later accounts.

events.x: Indenture at Berwick between John of Gaunt, styled king of Castile, as lieutenant in the Marches, and Scottish commissioners.
The Scots take the castle while the earl of Northumberland is at parliament; he buys it back for 2,000 marks.
events.r: Walsingham (Riley) ii, c. p. 118 (taken by money paid to the under-keeper while Northumberland was at Parliament; he recovers it). The price of 2,000 marks is from later accounts.

events.x: 642 men mustered in the garrison company of Sir Degary Seys.
Robert de Claveryng appointed chancellor and chamberlain of Berwick, clerk of works and keeper of provisions and artillery.
Clement VII (Avignon) names the Trinitarian friars "of the Bridge of Berwick" as adherents of Urban VI, the Roman pope, and orders them removed from a Scottish church.
Thomas Mowbray, earl marshal, takes the East March and Berwick for five years at £3,000 a year in truce; to add 80 men-at-arms and 160 archers if the French land in force.

Boniface IX allows John de Werk, mayor, and other burgesses and their wives to gain the jubilee indulgence without travelling to Rome. Berwick followed the Roman pope; the rest of the diocese of St Andrews followed Avignon.
Aid to the town for its losses, impoverishment and falling population.
The burgesses, damaged "both from Scotland and Normandy" and by the loss of 170 sarplers of wool in Flanders, ask to ship 2,000 sacks of Northumberland wool at half custom.
Payments for a duel at Berwick between a Scottish esquire, Beverlee, and Walter Stratherne in an appeal of treason.
The king's son holds Berwick and the East March with 200 men-at-arms and 400 archers.
events.r: CDS iv, no. 669; Medieval Soldier: TNA E 101/43/26

events.x: Letters dated at Berwick 6-12 July 1405 after the castle, held for the rebel earl of Northumberland, surrendered under bombardment (the guns to verify).
events.r: CPR 1405-08, pp. 68, 76, 78; Scott 1888, c. p. 83 ("the first shot from a cannon of large bore demolished part of a tower")

events.x: The George of Veere, laden at Berwick with wool, hides and fells by John Werk and other Berwick merchants for Middelburg in Zeeland, is driven into an English port.
The burgesses ask for the rest of 1,000 marks promised to rebuild their burnt town, of which they have had £33.
The burgesses remind the duke of Bedford, regent of France, that Henry V let them buy wool, skins and fells anywhere between Coquet and Tweed and Teviotdale and ship them overseas.
English complaints under the truce to be lodged with the mayor of Berwick, Scottish with the prior of Coldingham.

events.t: A Lucca broker in the garrison
events.x: Protection for Gerard Galganet of Lucca, merchant and broker of Southampton, as staying with Henry Percy, captain of Berwick.
In Richard Holland's Buke of the Howlat the owl becomes the fairest bird "Fro Burone to Berwike": from Orkney to the Tweed, the bounds of the realm.
events.r: Scottish Alliterative Poems, ed. Amours, STS (1897), Howlat l. 896

events.x: Payment for messages to the earl of Northumberland at the raising of the siege of Berwick.
On the petition of the mayor and burgesses, funds granted for repairing the walls of town and castle.
Margaret of Anjou hands Berwick to the Scots in return for support after Towton.
events.r: Hardyng (Ellis), p. 406 (Henry VI "gaue the toune and castell to the Scottes"). The day, 25 April, is the conventional modern date; Scott 1888 notes no surviving account of the exact date.

events.x: Statute confining wool exports to the Calais Staple saves the accustomed privileges of the burgesses of Berwick.
Brice Strayton, John Williamson and Thomas Williamson, all of Berwick-upon-Tweed and classed as Scots, receive licences to remain in England.
A prophecy under Thomas of Erceldoune's name addresses the town: "Though thou be subiect to the Saxons, sorrow thou not, / Thou shall be loosed at the last". Its cipher gives the year 1480.
The castle surrenders; Berwick is English thereafter.
events.r: Scott 1888, ch. VI (town retaken in 1482, the castle surrendering later); the day, 24 Aug., is the conventional date

events.x: The Scots tale opens with a portrait of the town: stone walls, double ditches, a castle with towers and portcullis, "the grit croce kirk, and eik the Masone Dew", the Jacobin and Carmelite friars.
Sir Thomas Darcy, captain of Berwick, is also made treasurer and chamberlain of the town and customer of the port.
On the princess's progress north to marry James IV, the captain's minstrels play on the gate of Berwick.
events.r: Ritson, Ancient Engleish Metrical Romanceës (1802) i, introduction, citing John Young's account

She requests a grant of part of the victuals to be taken at Newcastle whereof she is able to live.
petitions.end: Coram rege.

petitions.req: Walton requests that the king will grant her sustenance in a priory or abbey as her husband long served the king and his father in the wars in Wales and Scotland, and he was killed when Berwick fell because he did not wish to flee the town, and the enemy took what she had and bills of the arrears of her late husband's arrears of wages.
petitions.end: Coram rege et consilio.

petitions.end: Coram rege.

petitions.end: Coram rege et consilio.

petitions.end: Coram rege et consilio.

petitions.end: Coram rege.

petitions.req: Hayward requests remedy as the mayor and other burgesses of Berwick are obliged to him in 80 marks by a recognizance for passage, pesage and tronage in Berwick which amounts to 300 marks before the town fell, but he has been unable to have a writ from the English Chancery for the debt to be met from the goods of the burgesses wherever they are in England.1).
petitions.end: It is necessary that this remain until something can be ordained.2) Coram magno consilio.
petitions.hl: A creditor of the mayor and burgesses for passage, pesage and tronage "before the town fell" seeks his money.

petitions.req: Horseleye requests payment for the time that he was keeper of Berwick and Bamburgh castles, and that the king will ordain his will on the keeping of Bamburgh castle, and he complains that he has not received anything from a grant of 40 marks a year from the bailiwick of Bamburgh as the king has pardoned the men there.
petitions.end: It is to be expedited.

petitions.req: The Prior of Malton states that Thomas, son of Roger Petiwill of Scarborough, who held a messuage in Scarborough of the Prior, went to Berwick-upon-Tweed as a merchant when the town was in the king's hand, and died there without an heir of his blood. The messuage should return to the Prior as his escheat, but was taken into the king's hand on the assumption that Thomas had died with the Scots as the king's enemy, alt
petitions.end: The inquisition is to be examined, and if it is sufficient, as is supposed, justice is to be done to him in Chancery.

petitions.who: Simon de Rosse, son of Wadyn de Rosse
petitions.req: Simon, son of Wadyn de Rosse, states that his father served the King and his father for thirty years and more, in Gascony, Wales and Scotland; and that he lost goods and lands in the Scottish war, and was captured and beheaded at Berwick, leaving Simon and his four brothers and sisters destitute. He requests some aid from the King in some abbey or elsewhere where it might please the King.
petitions.end: Coram rege.Advice is to be taken on the place; and the King is to be informed of this, and he will speak his will on it.

petitions.who: Cassandra de Rosse (Ross), widow of Wadyn de Ross, and executrix of his testament

petitions.end: She is to have a writ in Chancery to the Treasurer and Barons of the Exchequer to hear the complaint contained in the petition, and to do swift justice to the complainant.

petitions.who: John Cosyn (Cousin), valet of the king
petitions.req: Cosyn shows that he is owed his wages which are due for his service in the garrison of Berwick Castle. He requests that he be paid, or have assigned to him the manor of Holywell, or the manor of Stretton which are in the king's hand, until the sum owed is taken. He also requests that the king should have regard for the profits that Cosyn has lost from his lands in Northumberland after the battle of Stirling.1).
petitions.end: The king wishes to receive advice.2) Coram rege.

He had possession of these lands until they were taken into the king's hands by Dode, along with his goods which were there, even though he had never suffered forfeiture.
petitions.end: Coram Rege.

petitions.who: John de Penyngton, William de Mauser and Richard de Preston
petitions.req: John de Penyngton, William de Mauser and Richard de Preston state that they and others, to the number of twelve, were engaged to go to Berwick in the king's service, for the protection of the town, but that on their way there they were set upon and robbed by a group of malefactors, so that one of their number is in danger of death. They request redress and a remedy.
petitions.end: [None].

petitions.who: Fishmongers and victuallers of the City of London
petitions.req: The fishmongers and victuallers request that the governors and officers of the town of Berwick be directed not to introduce new usages and to allow them peacefully to buy victuals in the town as they have been accustomed to do free from disturbance and impediment.
petitions.end: [None].

petitions.req: William Boynton requests the restoration of lands in Snainton, held in the time of Edward I by Ingelram and Margaret de Boynton, of whom he is the heir following the death of his elder brother. These lands were seized into the hands of Henry IV after the death of their mother, who held them in dower, due to the forfeiture of their father, Henry, for his involvement in a rising at Berwick in July 1405.
petitions.end: [None].

petitions.who: John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford, Regent of France
petitions.req: John, Duke of Bedford states that he was given the office of constable of the castle of Berwick-upon-Tweed by Henry IV, and that this gift was confirmed by Henry V and by the present king; but because he is Regent of France he cannot attend to this personally, and fears that this may put the castle in danger. He asks the king to grant, by authority of the present parliament, that he might appoint a lieutenant or lieu

petitions.req: The burgesses state that Henry V granted to them by his letters patent because of the damage to their town, and the scarcity of people that they could buy wool, skins and wool fells from whomever they like between Coquet and Tweed, and between Teviotdale, shipping them overseas paying for them at a reduced rate. The present king has for the six years following granted that they could only ship the wool to Middelburg
petitions.end: [None].
petitions.hl: The burgesses write to the duke of Bedford, regent of France, about their wool privilege between Coquet and Tweed.

petitions.who: Inhabitants of the East and West Marches towards Scotland
petitions.req: The people of the Scottish Marches request that the King appoint a great and mighty lord to organise the defence of the marches, as the Scots have recently increased raids across the border, have besieged Roxburgh and will soon attack Berwick.
petitions.end: [on face] For the chancellor, 6 February.Let it be sent to the Lords.It was delivered for the chancellor and read in the presence of the King 6 February.
